**exp-001 N-scaling evidence** (SciERC, n=200 subset, ⚠️ needs full-set confirmation):
- RE N=16: voting_conf ρ=0.448 (vs N=8 0.340, +0.108), SJ ρ=0.333 (vs 0.244, +0.089), all signals improve +0.07~0.10
- NER N=16: flat (already saturated at N=8) — voting_conf 0.401 vs 0.392
- **Key insight**: The task-complexity boundary is partially a SAMPLE BUDGET boundary. Compound error propagation increases per-instance variance, requiring more samples (N=16 vs N=8) to average out noise. This makes Claim 2 more nuanced: RE consistency fails at N=8 not because the signal is absent, but because it's noisier and needs more samples to manifest.
- ⚠️ Caveat: exp-001 ran on 200/529 instances. Full-set replication needed before claiming in paper.

## Story Spine (D072 — Universal Gap with Controlled Evidence)

**Problem**: Test-time scaling via multi-sample generation improves LLM reasoning, but its effectiveness for structured information extraction is unclear. Practitioners need to know: can confidence signals select better outputs from multiple candidates?

**Existing approaches & gaps**: Self-consistency (Wang et al. 2023) succeeds for discrete-answer reasoning. MBR decoding succeeds for MT. But structured IE outputs (entity sets, relation triples) present a fundamentally different challenge — and prior work conflates quality estimation with selection.

+\section{Thinking Token Impact Analysis}\label{app:thinking_token}
+Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks prepended to each response (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
+We quantify the potential impact on LP scores through three complementary arguments.
+\paragraph{LP shift magnitude.}
+The 4--5 thinking tokens contribute an estimated LP shift of 0.001 nats to the per-token log-probability average, representing 2.68\% of the median within-instance LP range (0.041 nats).
+This shift is too small to alter LP-based rankings.
+\paragraph{Constant prefix cancellation.}
+All $N$ samples within an instance share the same prompt and, under constrained decoding, the same absence of thinking tokens at inference time.
+Any LP bias from the training-time thinking prefix is therefore a near-constant additive shift across all candidates within an instance, leaving within-instance LP \textit{rankings} unchanged.
+\paragraph{CoNLL control group.}
+CoNLL and WNUT-17 checkpoints were trained without thinking tokens (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}).
+If thinking tokens caused LP compression on SciERC, CoNLL should exhibit lower tied fractions.
+Instead, CoNLL shows \textit{higher} tied fractions (95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$, vs.\ SciERC 60.3\% at $T{=}1.0$), directly contradicting the thinking-token hypothesis.

Under constrained decoding, log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, limiting per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}, Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}).

Our evaluation covers three datasets but only one RE benchmark (SciERC), where 40\% of instances receive zero F1, compressing the discriminable range and limiting signal differentiation for relation extraction.
RE selection failure persists even when restricting to non-zero F1 instances (Appendix~\ref{app:re_conditional_selection}), ruling out floor effects as the sole explanation, but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
WNUT-17 confirms the capability boundary of our approach, but our positive results on formal-domain text (CoNLL, SciERC) have not been validated on informal or noisy text where models achieve non-trivial performance.

We evaluate two model families (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B), both at 8B parameters.
A 3-seed robustness analysis confirms that signal rankings are stable across seeds ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), but whether our findings---particularly the correlation-selection gap and the difficulty-dependent signal ordering---hold for larger models (70B+) or closed-source APIs remains untested.
Larger models may produce higher-quality and more diverse samples, potentially altering the signal landscape.

Our analysis of selection potential uses only unsupervised signals.
We do not train a dedicated verifier or reward model, leaving unknown how much of the oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; $N{=}8$ was chosen to balance signal quality against compute cost, as $N$-scaling analysis shows sublinear gains beyond this point (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
The behavior at larger sample sizes (e.g., $N{=}64$) is unknown, and $N$-scaling gains are setting-dependent.

On CoNLL with LLaMA, the SJ--FK gap is only 0.003 ($\rho{=}0.431$ vs.\ $0.428$), so the structural advantage over surface signals may not generalize to all simple-schema datasets.
Our free-form ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP score compression persists without constrained decoding, but was conducted on a single dataset (SciERC) with one model (Qwen3-8B); whether the compression finding generalizes to other datasets, model families, or model scales remains untested.

Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with \texttt{enable\_thinking} active, injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens, no reasoning chain) before each response; CoNLL and WNUT checkpoints disabled this feature.
At inference time, constrained decoding suppresses thinking tokens in all configurations.
The 4--5 empty thinking tokens are diluted to ${<}0.3\%$ of the 1500+ token average training response, and the blocks contain no reasoning content, limiting any distributional shift to the first-token position.
Since LP selection fails across all datasets including CoNLL and WNUT-17 (which lack this confound), the thinking token inconsistency is unlikely to explain the correlation-selection gap.

413	
414	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks prepended to each response (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
415	We quantify the potential impact on LP scores through three complementary arguments.
416

418	The 4--5 thinking tokens contribute an estimated LP shift of 0.001 nats to the per-token log-probability average, representing 2.68\% of the median within-instance LP range (0.041 nats).
419	This shift is too small to alter LP-based rankings.
420	
421	\paragraph{Constant prefix cancellation.}
422	All $N$ samples within an instance share the same prompt and, under constrained decoding, the same absence of thinking tokens at inference time.

424

427	If thinking tokens caused LP compression on SciERC, CoNLL should exhibit lower tied fractions.
428	Instead, CoNLL shows \textit{higher} tied fractions (95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$, vs.\ SciERC 60.3\% at $T{=}1.0$), directly contradicting the thinking-token hypothesis.

433	The median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats---below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used throughout, providing data-driven justification for this cutoff rather than an arbitrary choice.

Our evaluation covers three datasets but only one RE benchmark (SciERC), where 40\% of instances receive zero F1, compressing the discriminable range and limiting signal differentiation for relation extraction.
RE selection failure persists even when restricting to non-zero F1 instances (Appendix~\ref{app:re_conditional_selection}), ruling out floor effects as the sole explanation, but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
WNUT-17 confirms the capability boundary of our approach, but our positive results on formal-domain text (CoNLL, SciERC) have not been validated on informal or noisy text where models achieve non-trivial performance.

We evaluate two model families (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B), both at 8B parameters.
A 3-seed robustness analysis confirms that signal rankings are stable across seeds ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), but whether our findings---particularly the correlation-selection gap and the difficulty-dependent signal ordering---hold for larger models (70B+) or closed-source APIs remains untested.
Larger models may produce higher-quality and more diverse samples, potentially altering the signal landscape.

Our analysis of selection potential uses only unsupervised signals.
We do not train a dedicated verifier or reward model, leaving unknown how much of the oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; $N{=}8$ was chosen to balance signal quality against compute cost, as $N$-scaling analysis shows sublinear gains beyond this point (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
The behavior at larger sample sizes (e.g., $N{=}64$) is unknown, and $N$-scaling gains are setting-dependent.

On CoNLL with LLaMA, the SJ--FK gap is only 0.003 ($\rho{=}0.431$ vs.\ $0.428$), so the structural advantage over surface signals may not generalize to all simple-schema datasets.
Our free-form ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP score compression persists without constrained decoding, but was conducted on a single dataset (SciERC) with one model (Qwen3-8B); whether the compression finding generalizes to other datasets, model families, or model scales remains untested.

2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on three English IE benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} contains 551 test instances annotated for joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types).
10	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} provides 3{,}453 test sentences with 4 entity types, where models achieve ${\approx}$91\% micro F1.
11	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} consists of 1{,}287 social media instances with emerging entities, used to probe method boundaries (52\% zero F1).
12	
13	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
14	Both \textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are fine-tuned with LoRA (rank$=$32, $\alpha{=}64$) for 5 epochs using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} under identical training procedures, ensuring comparisons across the two model families (both at 8B scale) reflect model differences rather than training confounds.
15	We note a training confound for SciERC: Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), which prepends empty \texttt{<think>\textbackslash n</think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) to each training response and includes them in the loss computation; CoNLL-2003 and WNUT-17 checkpoints explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}.
16	No reasoning content is present (the blocks are always empty), and constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, so thinking tokens do not appear in generated samples.
17	This constitutes a minor train--test distribution mismatch for SciERC ($<$0.3\% of the 2048-token training window); CoNLL-2003 and WNUT-17 are unaffected.
18	We discuss implications in the Limitations section.
19	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary; single seed, seed${=}42$), with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments.\footnote{$N{=}8$ establishes the primary baseline at minimal compute cost; $N{=}16$ with multiple seeds verifies scaling behavior. $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}) shows sublinear gains beyond $N{=}8$. $N{=}16$ results in Table~\ref{tab:robustness} (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}); 3-seed stability ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}, Appendix~\ref{app:multiseed}) confirms identical signal rankings across seeds.}
20	Quality estimation uses Spearman $\rho$ and AUROC; downstream utility uses best-of-$N$ selection macro F1 (instance-averaged) with exact span matching (NER) and head-tail-label matching (RE).
21	Inference uses vLLM with constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.
22

24	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}
25	\label{sec:qe_results}
26	
27	\begin{table*}[t]
28	\centering
29	\small
30	\caption{Quality estimation across tasks and models (Spearman $\rho$ and AUROC; $N{=}8$, seed${=}42$). Best value per column in \textbf{bold}. SciERC evaluates joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types, single benchmark---preliminary); CoNLL evaluates NER (4 types). $N{=}16$ results appear in Table~\ref{tab:robustness} (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).}

33	\toprule

Selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}).}
56	
57	\paragraph{Difficulty-dependent signal complementarity.}
58	On SciERC NER (6 types), structural signals lead: VC $\rho{=}0.379$, SJ $\rho{=}0.360$, both outperforming surface ($\rho{\leq}0.295$) and LP ($\rho{=}0.205$); on RE, VC extends this advantage ($\rho{=}0.350$; preliminary), but the remaining hierarchy reverses: multi-seed analysis shows LP rises above both SJ and FK (Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), likely because RE's 40\% zero-F1 rate creates a binary-outcome regime where generation confidence outperforms structural overlap.
59	The best NER AUROC reaches 0.816 (EM, CoNLL Qwen), indicating strong binary discriminative power; pairwise bootstrap CIs confirm the SJ--LP gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$, CI excludes zero) but the SJ--EM gap is marginal (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
60	
61	\paragraph{$\rho$--AUROC dissociation.}
62	Signal choice depends on use case: on CoNLL, EM leads AUROC (0.816) despite a middling $\rho$ (0.451), preferred for binary triage; this dissociation replicates across configurations (LP leads AUROC at 0.761 on CoNLL LLaMA yet trails in $\rho$).

64	\paragraph{Signal rankings shift with task difficulty.}
65	On CoNLL (greedy F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads ($\rho{=}0.451$, AUROC${=}0.816$); this crossover---EM${>}$SJ on easy tasks vs.\ SJ${>}$EM on hard tasks---demonstrates difficulty-dependent complementarity, consistent across model families.
66	On WNUT-17 (52\% zero F1), full-set VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ but conditional $\rho{=}0.038$ (n.s.; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$); all conditional signals collapse, suggesting a capability boundary beyond which consistency captures binary success/failure but not quality gradation.

73	\label{sec:selection_gap}
74

76	\centering
77	\small
78	\caption{Best-of-$N$ selection F1 on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). NER: 2-seed mean${\pm}\sigma$ ($n{=}551$), Fisher combined $p$ vs.\ greedy; RE: single seed (preliminary). Best non-oracle in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Greedy: a fixed $T{=}1.0$ sample (not $T{=}0$), serving as the no-selection reference. VC selection uses majority-threshold voting ($\text{freq}{>}N/2$; see \S\ref{sec:signals}).}
79	\label{tab:selection}
80	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
81	\toprule
82	Method & NER F1 & $p$ & RE F1 \\
83	\midrule
84	Oracle & $0.778 \pm 0.003$ & --- & 0.585 \\
85	\midrule
86	LP           & $\mathbf{0.647} \pm 0.005$ & .29 & 0.395 \\
87	\midrule
88	SJ           & $0.646 \pm 0.002$ & .68 & 0.386 \\
89	FK           & $0.646 \pm 0.001$ & .79 & --- \\

98	
99	Despite strong quality estimation, confidence signals yield limited gains when used for best-of-$N$ selection (Table~\ref{tab:selection}; see also Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}).
100	Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input regardless of which sample is evaluated; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
101	The non-trivial question is whether log-probability---the only per-sample signal---can exploit the oracle headroom.
102	We anchor this analysis on SciERC, where output diversity is substantial (39--43\% unique outputs per instance, F1 std 0.11--0.14; Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
103	
104	\paragraph{No significant improvement over greedy.}
105	We evaluate significance via 2-seed instance-level sign tests ($n{=}551$, Fisher combination).
106	On NER, the oracle (0.778) reveals 13.3~pp of headroom above greedy (0.645).
107	LP achieves the highest mean selection F1 (0.647), indistinguishable from greedy ($\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$); all other signals also fail to reach significance (all $p{>}0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}), with 75--80\% of instances producing identical F1 under signal selection and greedy.

113	
114	\paragraph{Quality estimation $\neq$ output selection.}
115	Instance-level confidence signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} among $N$ candidates is best.
116	When per-sample variance is low relative to instance-level difficulty, even perfect quality estimation cannot discriminate among near-identical candidates.
117	This gap has direct consequences for test-time scaling in IE \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}: closing it likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}.

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and selecting via agreement---yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but information extraction (IE) produces \textit{sets} of entities and relations with partial overlap, where no majority vote exists.

Across three NER benchmarks and one RE benchmark (preliminary, single dataset) with two 8B-parameter models, all signals achieve strong quality estimation yet none significantly improves sample selection despite substantial oracle headroom---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.

Signal rankings shift with task difficulty and collapse at the capability boundary.

Closing the gap likely requires learned per-sample scoring such as trained verifiers.

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
4	On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
5	More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
6	These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
7	For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
8	But information extraction (IE) poses a structurally different challenge.
9	The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
10	There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a structurally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{yao2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, finding results that our quality-estimation analysis corroborates.
Our work complements theirs in three directions: (i)~structural matching beyond surface-level agreement, (ii)~testing whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection (it does not), and (iii)~a difficulty gradient revealing non-obvious findings invisible on a single dataset.

Structured IE requires schema-compliant output, making constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} the standard inference strategy---without it, a substantial fraction of outputs from general-purpose models are unparseable.\footnote{Fine-tuned models may retain format compliance without grammar constraints: our free-form ablation achieves 99.95\% valid JSON rate (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).}
All experiments use constrained decoding, the regime under which structured IE is practically deployed.

Our central finding is the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): consistency-based signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82) but fail at sample selection despite substantial oracle headroom.
Four of five signals are instance-level by construction---this is definitional, not empirical.
Both per-sample mechanisms that could bridge the gap fail: MBR utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), and log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, though where compression is mitigated, selection recovers significant gains (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: high inter-sample agreement correlates with high F1 (quality estimation). \textbf{Right}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all candidates, precluding sample selection.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting confidence [VC], Soft Jaccard [SJ]), surface (exact match [EM], Fleiss' $\kappa$ [FK]), and model-internal (log-probability [LP])---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Metric dissociation.}
    We find that quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) decouple: different signals lead on different metrics, so single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.

    \item \textbf{The correlation-selection gap.}
    Despite strong quality estimation, no signal significantly improves sample selection despite substantial oracle headroom: log-probability scores are too compressed within instances to discriminate among candidates, and MBR-style consensus-proximity selection correlates with F1 across instances but not within them.

    \item \textbf{Difficulty- and task-dependent signal rankings.}
    Signal rankings shift with task complexity and task type---structural signals lead on NER while LP leads on RE---and collapse at the capability boundary (WNUT-17).
    NER findings span three datasets; RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone (preliminary).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a structurally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{yao2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, finding results that our quality-estimation analysis corroborates.
Our work complements theirs in three directions: (i)~structural matching beyond surface-level agreement, (ii)~testing whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection (it does not), and (iii)~a difficulty gradient revealing non-obvious findings invisible on a single dataset.

Structured IE requires schema-compliant output, making constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} the standard inference strategy---without it, a substantial fraction of outputs from general-purpose models are unparseable.\footnote{Fine-tuned models may retain format compliance without grammar constraints: our free-form ablation achieves 99.95\% valid JSON rate (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).}
All experiments use constrained decoding, the regime under which structured IE is practically deployed.

Our central finding is the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): consistency-based signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82) but fail at sample selection despite substantial oracle headroom.
Four of five signals are instance-level by construction---this is definitional, not empirical.
Both per-sample mechanisms that could bridge the gap fail: MBR utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), and log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, though where compression is mitigated, selection recovers significant gains (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: high inter-sample agreement correlates with high F1 (quality estimation). \textbf{Right}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all candidates, precluding sample selection.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting confidence [VC], Soft Jaccard [SJ]), surface (exact match [EM], Fleiss' $\kappa$ [FK]), and model-internal (log-probability [LP])---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Metric dissociation.}
    We find that quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) decouple: different signals lead on different metrics, so single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.

    \item \textbf{The correlation-selection gap.}
    Despite strong quality estimation, no signal significantly improves sample selection despite substantial oracle headroom: log-probability scores are too compressed within instances to discriminate among candidates, and MBR-style consensus-proximity selection correlates with F1 across instances but not within them.

    \item \textbf{Difficulty- and task-dependent signal rankings.}
    Signal rankings shift with task complexity and task type---structural signals lead on NER while LP leads on RE---and collapse at the capability boundary (WNUT-17).
    NER findings span three datasets; RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone (preliminary).
\end{enumerate}

The gap holds even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
